author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen offers selective exegetical notes on difficult verses in Leviticus, explaining their spiritual and practical meaning for Christian readers.
argument: Origen interprets Leviticus to show that a particular kind of unintentional sin—keeping a command one should not keep under a pretext of piety—requires sacrifice, while deliberate action does not. He argues that the wording of the purification law prophetically safeguards Mary from being thought unclean, both because she bore a male child without insemination and because she was not simply a woman but a virgin. He explains the public marking of lepers as a model for church discipline, distinguishes feasts from solemn assemblies, and reads the evergreen branches of the Feast of Tabernacles as signs of unfading grace and hope in Christ. Finally, he clarifies the redemption rules for vowed houses and fields, including their reversion at the Jubilee.

outline.move: Explains unintentional sin as keeping a command one should not keep under a pretext of piety, and shows that the sin offering itself is called 'sin', so Christ can be called sin as the one sacrificed for all.

Argues that the phrase 'if she is inseminated' is included prophetically so that Mary, who bore a male child without insemination, would not be thought unclean; he adds that even without this phrase she would not be unclean because she was not simply a woman but a virgin.
Explains why the leper must go with uncovered head and torn clothes: so others can recognize and avoid the uncleanness, and compares this to apostolic commands to avoid disorderly or sinful brothers.
Distinguishes a 'feast' from a 'solemn assembly', and interprets the palm branches of the Feast of Tabernacles as signs of the unfading grace and hope restored to believers in Christ.
Explains the redemption of vowed houses and fields, including the added fifth, the restriction on selling to others, and the reversion of purchased fields at the Jubilee.

scripture: Origen cites the Septuagint (LXX) text of Leviticus and follows its book names and numbering. Psalm references follow LXX numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and note LXX numbering where it differs from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of composition of the Notes on Leviticus.
The identity of the addressee or original audience.
Whether the work was originally a continuous commentary or a collection of scholia.
Whether 'the Apostle' refers specifically to Paul, since the source uses only the generic title.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues that the wording of the purification law prophetically safeguards Mary from being thought unclean, both because she bore a male child without insemination and because she was not simply a woman but a virgin.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλʼ ἐφίστημι μήποτε ἵνα προφητικῶς ἡ Μαρία, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ ἐσπερματίσθαι (17) τεκοῦσα ἄρσεν, μὴ νομισθῇ ἀκάθαρτος εἶναι, γεγεννηκυῖα τὸν Σωτῆρα, εἴρηκεν ὅλον Ἐδύνατο δὲ καὶ μὴ προκειμένου τοῦ, Ἐὰν σπερματισθῇ, νοεῖσθαι μὴ οὖσα ἀκάθαρτος ἡ Μαρία· οὐ γὰρ ἀπλῶς γυνὴ, ἀλλὰ παρθένος.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen raises two distinct points: first, he speculates that the phrase 'if she is inseminated' was included prophetically so that Mary, who bore a male child without insemination, would not be thought unclean; second, he adds that even without this phrase, Mary would not be unclean because she was not simply a woman but a virgin. The brief conflates these as a single argument and overstates certainty ('argues' vs. 'speculates/raises the possibility').

_unresolved_facts.claim: Finally, he clarifies the redemption rules for vowed houses and fields, including their reversion at the Jubilee.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸν δὲ ἐξ ἀγορασίας ἀγρὸν ἀγοράσας, οὐκ ἀνακτήσεται τοῦτον ἑαυτῷ· ἀλλὰ πρὸς λόγον ἀποδοὺς τὸν καρπὸν τῷ Θεῷ, ἐν τῷ Ἰωβὴλ ἀποκαταστήσεται τὸν ἀγρὸν τῷ πεπρακότι.
_unresolved_facts.fix: For purchased fields, Origen states the opposite of 'reversion' to the original vower: the field is restored to the one who sold it (τῷ πεπρακότι), not to the person who vowed it. The brief's 'reversion at the Jubilee' is accurate only for the general pattern, but misleading for the purchased-field case which Origen specifically addresses.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Explains unintentional sin as keeping a command one should not keep under a pretext of piety, and shows that the sin offering itself is called 'sin', so Christ can be called sin as the one sacrificed for all.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς ὁ γεγονὼς Ἰουδαῖος, ἵνα Ἰουδαίους κερδήσῃ, καὶ περιτεμὼν τὸν Τιμόθεον... Οὕτω δυνατὸν τὸν Χριστὸν καλεῖν ἀμαρείαν, ὡς ὑπὸρ τῆς πάντων ἁμαρτίας τυθέντα.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline omits the example of Paul becoming a Jew to win Jews and circumcising Timothy, which is central to the argument about doing what is not required under a pretext of piety. It also misspells 'ἁμαρτίαν' as 'ἀμαρείαν' in the source (though this may be a textual variant).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Explains the redemption of vowed houses and fields, including the added fifth, the restriction on selling to others, and the reversion of purchased fields at the Jubilee.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὸν δὲ ἐξ ἀγορασίας ἀγρὸν ἀγοράσας, οὐκ ἀνακτήσεται τοῦτον ἑαυτῷ· ἀλλὰ πρὸς λόγον ἀποδοὺς τὸν καρπὸν τῷ Θεῷ, ἐν τῷ Ἰωβὴλ ἀποκαταστήσεται τὸν ἀγρὸν τῷ πεπρακότι.
_unresolved_facts.fix: For purchased fields, the field reverts to the seller (τῷ πεπρακότι), not to the one who vowed it. The outline should specify that purchased fields revert to the original seller, not simply 'reversion of purchased fields at the Jubilee' which implies reversion to the vower.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Timothy - Companion of Paul, circumcised by Paul to win Jews, cited as an example of doing something not required under a pretext of piety.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς ὁ γεγονὼς Ἰουδαῖος, ἵνα Ἰουδαίους κερδήσῃ, καὶ περιτεμὼν τὸν Τιμόθεον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is the one who 'became a Jew to win Jews' (ὁ γεγονὼς Ἰουδαῖος, ἵνα Ἰουδαίους κερδήσῃ) and who circumcised Timothy. Timothy is the object of the action, not the example of someone doing something not required under a pretext of piety. The example is Paul, with Timothy as the one acted upon.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Apostle (quoted) - Introduced by 'thus the Apostle said about sinners' (Οὕτω ὁ Ἀπόστολος περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων ἔφη); the first citation is given without explicit quotation formula, the second is quoted directly.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὕτως ὁ Ἀπόστολος περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτανόντων ἔφη· Στέλλεσθε ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ παντὸς ἀδελφοῦ ἀτάκτως περιπατοῦντος, καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὴν παράδοσιν, ἣν παρελάβετε παῤ ἡμῶν· καὶ, Ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος, ἢ πόρνος, ἢ πλεονέκτης, ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης, ἢ μέθυσος, ἢ λοίδορος, ἢ ἅρπαξ· τῷ τοιούτῳ μὴ συνεσθίειν (18).
_unresolved_facts.fix: Both citations are introduced by the same formula: the first is introduced with 'Στέλλεσθε ὑμᾶς...' directly following ἔφη, and the second is introduced with 'καὶ, Ἐάν τις...' The brief incorrectly states 'the first citation is given without explicit quotation formula.' Both have explicit quotation context; the first is a direct quotation, the second is also directly quoted with καὶ connecting it.
